challenges.name: reading-diffs-quiz
challenges.title: Read the hunk before you trust it
challenges.description: Two hunks from a coding agent's pull request: what a hunk header tells you about line numbers and size, and what a pair of identical - and + lines with a "No newline" marker really changed.

questions.explanation: True. In @@ -40,7 +40,9 @@ the part after + describes the new file: the hunk starts at line 40 and spans 9 lines, so lines 40 to 48. The part after - describes the old file: 7 lines from line 40. Both counts include the context lines (the ones starting with a space), which are the same on both sides: here 5 context lines, 2 removed (5 + 2 = 7) and 4 added (5 + 4 = 9), so the hunk is 2 lines longer than before. The misconception is that the numbers after the comma count only changed lines; they count every line of the hunk on that side, which is why you can check a hunk is complete by counting.

False. The removed line and the added line have the same text. The marker "\ No newline at end of file" belongs to the line just above it: in the old file, that last line had no line break after it. The new file ends with a line break, so Git shows the line as removed and added again, and --stat counts it as 1 insertion and 1 deletion. Nothing about the value changed. Agents and editors that rewrite whole files often add or drop the final newline or change line endings; that noise inflates the line counts and can hide the one hunk that matters. The misconception is that every -/+ pair is a change of content: compare the two lines character by character, and read the marker.

challenges.name: diff-file-summary
challenges.title: Summarise a diff before you read it
challenges.description: A coding agent's pull request on the CodeDev platform was approved as "a 20-line fix" to the progress bar, while the same diff deleted a database migration further down. The review bot now prints a summary of every file a diff touches before anyone reads the hunks. Write parseDiff(diff), which reads the text of one git diff (unified format, Git's default options; paths never contain spaces) and returns one entry per file, in order: path (the path after the change; a deleted file keeps the path it had), from (the old path when the file was renamed, otherwise null), status ("added" when the header has "new file mode", "deleted" for "deleted file mode", "renamed" when the two paths in "diff --git a/<old> b/<new>" differ, otherwise "modified", which includes mode-only changes), binary (true when Git printed "Binary files ... differ"), and added / removed: the number of lines starting with "+" / "-" inside the file's hunks (the lines after an "@@" header, until the next "diff --git" line). The "--- a/..." and "+++ b/..." header lines are not changes, but a changed line inside a hunk can itself start with "--", "++" or "diff --git". "\ No newline at end of file" and context lines (starting with a space) are not counted. Ignore any text before the first "diff --git" line; a text with none has no files. The test runner reads the diff from stdin and prints { files, totals } as JSON, with totals = { files, added, removed }.
hints: How does a human reader know whether a line that starts with "---" is the old-file header or a removed line? What has already happened in the file by the time each of them appears?

Split the text on "\n" and walk the lines with two pieces of state: the file you are filling in (none before the first "diff --git") and whether you have reached that file's first "@@". Before the first "@@" only header lines can appear (new file mode, deleted file mode, rename from/to, index, ---, +++, Binary files); after it, only the first character of each line matters.

A similar walk on a different diff: "diff --git a/docs/a.md b/docs/b.md", "similarity index 95%", "rename from docs/a.md", "rename to docs/b.md", "--- a/docs/a.md", "+++ b/docs/b.md", "@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@", "----", "+---", " # Title". The paths differ, so the entry is renamed with from docs/a.md and path docs/b.md. The "---" and "+++" lines come before the "@@", so they are headers. After the "@@", "----" is one removed line (its content is "---") and "+---" is one added line: 1 added, 1 removed.
